definition: The function $X(z) = \sum_n x[n] z^{-n}$ of a complex variable $z$ that packs a discrete-time signal $x[n]$ into one function on the complex plane.
The set of points $z$ where the z-transform sum converges absolutely. It is a ring $r_{in} < |z| < r_{out}$ bounded by poles, and together with the formula $X(z)$ it fixes the signal.
The complex plane of the variable $z$ of a z-transform. A point $z = \rho e^{j\omega}$ weights sample $n$ by $\rho^{-n} e^{-j\omega n}$.
The circle $|z| = 1$ in the complex plane. On it $z = e^{j\omega}$, and a z-transform becomes the discrete-time Fourier transform.

A point where a z-transform is infinite: a root of the denominator of a rational $X(z)$. The surface $|X(z)|$ shoots up there; a pole at $r e^{j\theta}$ in a causal signal means a term $r^n e^{j\theta n}$ in time.
A point where a z-transform is 0: a root of the numerator of a rational $X(z)$. A zero on the unit circle blocks that frequency completely.
$X(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_n x[n] e^{-j\omega n}$: the z-transform on the unit circle. It exists as an ordinary sum when the unit circle lies inside the region of convergence.
How strongly, and with what phase shift, a linear system passes a sinusoid of each frequency. For a discrete-time system it is $H(e^{j\omega})$, the transfer function on the unit circle.
A signal that is zero for $n < 0$, or a system whose impulse response is. Its region of convergence is the outside of a circle, including $z = \infty$.

A system is BIBO stable when every bounded input gives a bounded output, which holds exactly when $\sum_n |h[n]| < \infty$: the unit circle lies in the region of convergence. A causal system is stable when all its poles are inside the unit circle.
A signal that is zero before some time $n_0$. Its region of convergence is the outside of its outermost pole.
A signal that is zero after some time $n_0$. Its region of convergence is the inside of its innermost pole.
A signal that runs forever in both directions of time. Its region of convergence, if any, is a ring between two poles.
The signal $\delta[n]$: 1 at $n = 0$ and 0 everywhere else. Its z-transform is 1.
The signal $u[n]$: 1 for $n \ge 0$ and 0 before. Its z-transform is $1/(1 - z^{-1})$ for $|z| > 1$.
Getting $x[n]$ back from $X(z)$ and its region of convergence, by partial fractions, long division, or the contour integral $x[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi j}\oint X(z) z^{n-1} dz$ round a circle in the ROC.
Splitting a rational function into a sum of simple pieces, one per pole, so each can be inverted on its own.
A filter that removes one narrow band of frequencies. In discrete time, zeros on the unit circle at $\pm\theta$ block the frequency $\omega = \theta$ completely.
Reading $|X(z)|$ at a point as the gain times the product of the distances to the zeros divided by the product of the distances to the poles.
The output $h[n]$ of a linear time-invariant system when the input is the unit impulse. Its z-transform is the system's transfer function.

The function $X(s) = \int x(t)\, e^{-st}\, dt$ of a complex variable $s = \sigma + j\omega$ that packs a continuous-time signal $x(t)$ into one function on the complex plane. On the line $s = j\omega$ it becomes the Fourier transform.

The complex plane of the variable $s = \sigma + j\omega$ of a Laplace transform, with $\sigma$ across and $j\omega$ up. A point $s$ weights the signal at time $t$ by $e^{-st}$, an arrow that turns at $\omega$ and grows or shrinks at rate $\sigma$.

A point where a Laplace transform is infinite: a root of the denominator of a rational $X(s)$. A pole at $p$ contributes a term $e^{pt}$ to the signal, so its distance left of the imaginary axis sets the decay rate and its height sets the oscillation frequency.
A point where a Laplace transform is 0: a root of the numerator of a rational $X(s)$. A zero on the imaginary axis blocks that frequency completely.

The set of $s$ for which the Laplace integral converges. It is a vertical strip $\alpha < \operatorname{Re} s < \beta$, because the size of $e^{-st}$ depends only on $\operatorname{Re} s$, and it is bounded by poles.

The ratio $H(s) = Y(s)/X(s)$ of the Laplace transforms of output and input of a linear time-invariant system that starts at rest. It is the transform of the impulse response, and its values on the imaginary axis give the frequency response.
The inversion formula $x(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi j}\int_{c-j\infty}^{c+j\infty} X(s)\,e^{st}\,ds$, taken up a vertical line $\operatorname{Re} s = c$ inside the region of convergence.

The signal $x(t)$ recovered from $X(s)$ and its region of convergence, usually by partial fractions and a table, or by the Bromwich integral. The same formula with a different region gives a different signal.
For a causal signal with no impulse at the origin, $x(0^+) = \lim_{s\to\infty} sX(s)$: the starting value is the far-away height of $sX(s)$.
If every pole of $sX(s)$ is strictly in the left half-plane, then $x(\infty) = \lim_{s\to 0} sX(s)$: the value the signal settles to.
Convolution in time becomes multiplication of transforms: $(x*y)(t) \leftrightarrow X(s)Y(s)$, with a region containing the intersection of the two regions. In decibels the two surfaces add.

The transform $\int_{0^-}^{\infty} x(t)e^{-st}dt$, started just before the switch-on so that initial conditions enter through $\mathcal{L}\{x'\} = sX(s) - x(0^-)$. It is the form used to solve differential equations.

The number $\zeta$ in $s^2 + 2\zeta\omega_n s + \omega_n^2$, equal to the cosine of the angle between a pole and the negative real axis. Below 1 the system oscillates; at 1 it is critically damped; above 1 it is overdamped.
The number $\omega_n$ in $s^2 + 2\zeta\omega_n s + \omega_n^2$: the distance of the poles from the origin, and the frequency at which the system would oscillate with no damping.
For a pole at $-a$, the time $1/a$ in which the signal $e^{-at}$ falls to $1/e = 0.368$ of its value. For an RC circuit it is the product $RC$.
The case $\zeta = 1$ of a second-order system, a double pole on the negative real axis: the fastest return to rest without oscillation.

A peak in the frequency response where a pole pair near the imaginary axis passes close to the axis. Its height is about $1/(2a)$ for poles at $-a \pm j\omega_0$, so halving the distance $a$ doubles the peak.
The part of the s-plane with $\operatorname{Re} s < 0$. A causal system is stable exactly when all its poles are in it; under $z = e^{sT}$ it maps inside the unit circle.
For a simple pole $p$ of $F(s)$, the number $\lim_{s\to p}(s-p)F(s)$. The Bromwich integral is a sum of residues of $X(s)e^{st}$ at the poles on one side of the line.

The function $X(f) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)\,e^{-j2\pi f t}\,dt$ that says how much of each frequency $f$ a signal $x(t)$ contains, and with what phase. The inverse transform rebuilds $x(t)$ from $X(f)$.

The representation of a signal that repeats every $T$ seconds as a sum of turning arrows at multiples of $1/T$: $x(t) = \sum_k c_k e^{j2\pi k t/T}$ with $c_k = \frac1T\int_0^T x(t)e^{-j2\pi k t/T}dt$.
One of the sinusoids in a Fourier series, with frequency $k/T$ for a whole number $k$. The first harmonic, $k = 1$, is the fundamental, whose period is the period of the signal itself.
A plot of the amplitude $|c_k|$ (or $A_k$) and the phase $\angle c_k$ of each frequency component of a signal against frequency. It describes the same signal as the waveform, in terms of frequency.

The complex number $Ae^{j\varphi}$ that holds the amplitude and phase of a sinusoid $A\cos(\omega t + \varphi) = \operatorname{Re}[Ae^{j\varphi}e^{j\omega t}]$, leaving out the time dependence. Sinusoids of one frequency add by adding their phasors.

The frequency of an arrow $e^{-j\omega t}$ that turns clockwise. A real signal contains arrows at $+f$ and $-f$ with complex-conjugate coefficients, so its spectrum is mirror-symmetric and the negative half adds no information.

The fact that $\int_0^T e^{j2\pi k t/T}e^{-j2\pi m t/T}dt$ is $T$ when $k = m$ and $0$ otherwise. It is why the Fourier coefficient integral isolates one frequency and why Parseval's theorem has no cross terms.

A phase that is a straight line in frequency, $\varphi(f) = -2\pi f t_0$. It is the signature of a pure delay of $t_0$ seconds: amplitudes are unchanged and each frequency is shifted by the same time.
The statement that a signal's average power (or energy) is the same whether computed from the waveform or from its spectrum. For a periodic signal, $\frac1T\int_0^T x^2\,dt = \sum_k |c_k|^2$.

The overshoot of about $8.95\%$ of the jump that a partial Fourier sum shows next to a discontinuity. Adding harmonics narrows the overshoot and moves it toward the jump but does not reduce its height.

The function $\operatorname{sinc}(u) = \sin(\pi u)/(\pi u)$, with $\operatorname{sinc}(0) = 1$ and zeros at the nonzero integers. It is the Fourier transform of a rectangular pulse: $\operatorname{rect}(t/\tau)\leftrightarrow\tau\operatorname{sinc}(f\tau)$.
The rule that a signal cannot be narrow in both time and frequency: with RMS widths $\sigma_t$ and $\sigma_f$, $\sigma_t\sigma_f \ge 1/(4\pi)$, with equality for the Gaussian pulse.
The effect by which, after sampling at rate $f_s$, a frequency $f$ above $f_s/2$ gives the same samples as the lower frequency $|f - mf_s|$ and so cannot be told apart from it.
Twice the highest frequency in a signal, $2f_{\max}$. Sampling faster than this keeps every frequency within $0$ to $f_s/2$ and avoids aliasing.
Half the sampling rate, $f_s/2$: the highest frequency a sampled signal can represent. Components above it fold back below it.

The map from $N$ samples $x[n]$ to $N$ numbers $X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1}x[n]e^{-j2\pi kn/N}$, which are the DTFT sampled at $N$ equally spaced points round the unit circle. Bin $k$ stands for the frequency $kf_s/N$.
The spreading of a sinusoid's energy across many DFT bins when it does not complete a whole number of cycles in the window, because the repeated window then has a jump at each seam.

A smooth taper, such as the Hann window $0.5 - 0.5\cos(2\pi n/N)$, applied to the samples before a DFT so they approach zero at the ends. It lowers leakage far from the peak at the cost of a wider main lobe.

Any algorithm that computes the DFT in about $N\log_2 N$ operations rather than $N^2$. The radix-2 version splits the samples into even and odd halves repeatedly, and needs $\frac N2\log_2 N$ complex multiplications.
The unit complex number $W_N^k = e^{-j2\pi k/N}$ that multiplies one input of an FFT butterfly. Its key properties are $W_N^2 = W_{N/2}$ and $W_N^{k+N/2} = -W_N^k$.
The basic step of the radix-2 FFT: from inputs $a$ and $b$ it forms $a + Wb$ and $a - Wb$, using one multiplication for two outputs. Drawn with crossing lines, it looks like a butterfly.

The reordering of the input of an in-place radix-2 FFT so that sample $n$ sits at the position given by its index written in binary and read backwards. For $N = 8$, $x[1]$ goes to position 4 and $x[3]$ to 6.
